title: Hello World conformance slot
purpose: Historical classic Malbolge Hello World conformance slot: a clean halt with zero output.

title: Echo one byte demo
purpose: Bootstrap slot: proof that a real classic Malbolge program can pass verification.

title: Echo one byte
purpose: The smallest public candidate rung: synthesize a program that echoes the first input byte.

title: Echo two bytes
purpose: Extend echo-prefix synthesis from one byte to two bytes.

title: Echo four bytes
purpose: Longer straight-line copying with more room for agent mistakes.

title: Echo two bytes across multiple cases
purpose: Require one program to survive multiple hash-derived inputs.

title: Xor one byte
purpose: Apply the v0 xor-mask transform to the first byte.

title: Xor one byte with 4096-byte program cap
purpose: Same v0 xor-mask task as L2.R0.xor-1, with only the program-length cap relaxed for calibration.

title: Crazy-mask one byte
purpose: Apply output = crazy(input, 0x51) mod 256 to the first byte. The transform is per-trit realizable inside a CRAZY-chain dispatch, so this rung demands totality over all 256 inputs without XOR's binary-carry obstruction. It sits between the finite-map rungs and full xor-1.

title: Finite-map xor51 over two published bytes
purpose: Require one candidate to map the published bytes 0x02->0x53 and 0x06->0x57. This is finite-map calibration, not full byte-wide xor1.

title: Finite-map xor51 over four published bytes
purpose: Extend finite-map xor51 routing to four published one-byte inputs. This remains a published finite map, not hidden holdout generality.

title: Finite-map xor51 over six published bytes
purpose: Half-step between map4 and map8: the four map4 bytes plus the first two map8 extension bytes. Sized for single-dispatch routing with richer lane shapes.

title: Finite-map xor51 over seven published bytes (map8 minus 0xc0)
purpose: Fills the map6-to-map8 difficulty cliff from the easy side: the six map6 bytes plus 0xa7. Dispatch feasibility: 539 separating configs, against 1261 for map6 and 39 for map8 (measured with `malbolge-rungs feasibility`).

title: Finite-map xor51 over seven published bytes (map8 minus 0xa7)
purpose: The steep half of the map6-to-map8 cliff: the six map6 bytes plus 0xc0, the input that collapses dispatch separation. Dispatch feasibility: 50 separating configs, against 1261 for map6 and 39 for map8.

title: Finite-map xor51 over eight published bytes
purpose: Bridge known finite-map/routing evidence toward the full XOR frontier with eight published one-byte inputs.

title: Finite-map xor51 over twelve high-range bytes
purpose: Input-placement probe: twelve inputs drawn deterministically from 0x80..=0xff (sha256("mal51-fm-hi-v0:<counter>") first byte, filtered, deduplicated). High-range inputs admit identity-dispatch landings above the prefix/data zone, isolating routing capacity from the low-landing structural problem.

title: Finite-map xor51 over twelve low-range bytes
purpose: Input-placement probe: twelve inputs drawn deterministically from 0x00..=0x40 (sha256("mal51-fm-low-v0:<counter>") first byte, filtered, deduplicated). Same count as map12-hi but inputs whose natural landings collide with prefix and dispatch data, exercising the low-landing problem specifically.

title: Finite-map xor51 over sixteen published bytes
purpose: The largest v0 finite-map xor51 calibration rung. Passing it is meaningful routing evidence but still does not solve full byte-wide xor1.

title: Xor-mask coverage over at least 32 of 256 inputs
purpose: All 256 single-byte inputs are enumerated; the candidate must halt with the correct xor51 output on at least 32 of them. Mismatches and non-halting runs on other inputs are tolerated. This makes partial-coverage progress deterministic and measurable.

title: Xor-mask coverage over at least 34 of 256 inputs
purpose: Coverage-ladder step between cov32 and cov36: all 256 single-byte inputs, at least 34 exact xor51 outputs required, failures elsewhere tolerated. Added 2026-08-10 and strictly additive. 34 is the exhaustive ceiling of the branchless CRAZY/ROTATE family, so this step asks for that family's optimum realized in the machine; cov36 and up cannot be reached without input-dependent branching.

title: Xor-mask coverage over at least 36 of 256 inputs
purpose: Coverage-ladder step between cov32 and cov64: all 256 single-byte inputs, at least 36 exact xor51 outputs required, failures elsewhere tolerated.

title: Xor-mask coverage over at least 40 of 256 inputs
purpose: Coverage-ladder step between cov32 and cov64: all 256 single-byte inputs, at least 40 exact xor51 outputs required, failures elsewhere tolerated.

title: Xor-mask coverage over at least 48 of 256 inputs
purpose: Coverage-ladder step between cov32 and cov64: all 256 single-byte inputs, at least 48 exact xor51 outputs required, failures elsewhere tolerated.

title: Xor-mask coverage over at least 48 of 256 inputs, in 2048 bytes
purpose: Length-pressure variant of cov48, added 2026-08-10 and strictly additive. Same threshold, half the space: the shipped cov48 program scores 71/256 in 3178 bytes, so this rung asks for the same coverage in less room. It isolates program size as its own axis, which is what separates the 256-byte transform rungs from the 4096-byte coverage rungs.

title: Xor-mask coverage over at least 64 of 256 inputs
purpose: Same all-256 coverage scoring as cov32 with the threshold raised to 64. Passing it requires beating the shared-operand-pool ceiling of single-dispatch station architectures.

title: Reverse one byte
purpose: One-byte reverse is behaviorally trivial but useful as a transform-family sanity check.

title: Rotate one byte
purpose: Rotate the first input byte left by one bit.

title: Xor two bytes across multiple cases
purpose: Discourage constant-output shortcuts by requiring a transform over two cases.

title: Reverse two bytes across multiple cases
purpose: A small but real input-dependent transformation over several cases.

title: Xor four bytes with length pressure
purpose: Four-byte transform with a cap intended to expose brittle generated code.

title: Small mixed transform
purpose: Draft rung for compact deterministic byte remapping tasks.

title: Hash prefix one byte
purpose: A public finite lookup task. Five deterministic epochs fix five public input/target rows; the program is not given the seed, so clearing this shows a five-row map fits the machine, not that anything hash-like was computed.

title: Hash prefix one byte across multiple cases
purpose: A public finite lookup task: fifteen public input/target rows (five epochs, three cases). The program is not given the seed; nothing about hash computation is tested.

title: Hash prefix with length pressure
purpose: A public finite lookup task under length pressure: ten public input/target rows (five epochs, two cases) against a 256-byte program cap.

title: Future transform placeholder
purpose: Reserved for a future calibrated transform rung.

title: Future hash-prefix placeholder
purpose: Reserved for a future frontier hash-prefix rung after empirical calibration.

title: Xor-mask coverage over at least 96 of 256 inputs
purpose: Coverage-ladder step above cov64, added 2026-08-10 and strictly additive. The 4096-byte cap is raised to 8192 here on purpose: the cov48 solve reached 71/256 using 3178 of its 4096 bytes at ~45 bytes per correct case, so a 96-case threshold under the old cap would test whether the program fits rather than how far coverage reaches. Program size is isolated instead by the cov48-len2048 rung.

title: Echo the whole input, whatever its length
purpose: Every other rung on this ladder fixes the output width in its definition, so a candidate can be written straight-line: consume a known number of bytes, emit a known number back. This family is designed to pressure iteration instead. The input length is drawn from the challenge seed — the bounds are public, but the length of any given case is not knowable in advance — so the intended program reads until the input runs out: the VM sets a to the all-2s word on a read past the end, and that is the only signal it gets. That means a loop, and in classic Malbolge a loop is the hard part: every cell that executes is enciphered immediately afterwards, so the body is different code on its second pass and must either restore itself or ride the 94-cycle back to its starting values. Known to be possible — the published Malbolge programs that loop, from 99-bottles to the Nagoya LISP interpreter, all solve exactly this. The cases are deterministic and public (27 epochs of 3), so a pass does not prove a loop was used — a program could in principle dispatch on an identifying prefix and emit memorized answers — but unrolling by position is priced out: input up to 255 bytes against a 4096-byte cap leaves about 16 bytes per position, far under what an IN plus an end-of-input test plus a conditional jump plus an OUT costs under loader validity. Python: print(input()). The intended minimum: read a byte, emit it, repeat until the input ends.

purpose: Every other rung on this ladder fixes the output width in its definition, so a candidate can be written straight-line: consume a known number of bytes, emit a known number back. This family is designed to pressure iteration instead. The input length is drawn from the challenge seed — the bounds are public, but the length of any given case is not knowable in advance — so the intended program reads until the input runs out: the VM sets a to the all-2s word on a read past the end, and that is the only signal it gets.
